title: Stock Monitoring Tool
text:
Draft
The Stock Monitoring Tool (SMT), developed by FAO, is an R-Shiny application hosted on the iMarine gateway (D4Science), with remote computing resources. It lets users with little or no programming experience run data-limited methods to evaluate and monitor stock status, and it is the main training environment of the toolbox: courses use the SMT to run a method, and the toolbox pages to understand its data needs, assumptions, diagnostics and misuse risks. Source code: fdiwg/smt-shiny.

title: Stock Monitoring Tool
text:
Workflow in the app
Each method has an Introduction page (background and links to the FAO SDG 14.4.1 eLearning module), a Data tab (format and data considerations), a Workflow tab, and a Sample dataset page that doubles as the input template. Users upload data, set parameters (with information buttons on each field), run the method, and download a report; reports are also saved to the user’s private workspace. Run time with the sample datasets is 1–3 minutes.

title: Stock Monitoring Tool
text:
Use and misuse






WarningBefore using SMT results for advice




Sample datasets are for practice. The JABBA sample file, for example, is synthetic and not a validated assessment.
Default settings are not a recommendation. Priors, growth parameters and selectivity must be justified for the stock; check each method’s misuse-prevention section in this toolbox.
Diagnostics are not optional. A run that completes is not a converged or validated assessment; report the diagnostics and sensitivity runs listed on the method page.
Keep the record. Save data, settings and the report, so the run can be reviewed and repeated.

Running it locally
The repository includes a Dockerfile and an renv.lock that pin the R packages (including JABBA 2.3.7 and its JAGS dependency), so the app can be deployed for a national institute or a course without the iMarine gateway.

title: Method selector
text:
Answer the questions about the stock and the data you have. The selector lists the methods whose data requirements you meet, the ones you don’t (and why), and misuse warnings for your situation. It is a screening aid in the spirit of FishPath: it narrows the options and flags risks, and it does not replace diagnostics or working-group review.






NoteHow the selector decides





Each tool’s data requirements are recorded in data/methods.csv, and each warning is a rule in data/misuse_rules.csv. Do not use means a core assumption is violated by the data you describe. Caution means the method can be used, but only with the extra checks named in the warning. The rules are a first draft for review.

Install Rtools
For any R version of 4.3.x, you need to select to install Rtools 43 and for R version 4.4.x, you need to install Rtools 44 Rtools. An exe file will be downloaded. Click on it and follow instructions.

section: SPiCT: Surplus Production models in Continuous-Time
text:
SPiCT: Surplus Production models in Continuous-Time
SPiCT is an R-package for fitting surplus production models in continuous-time to fisheries catch data and biomass indices.
This package requires the installation of TMB and Rtools. Fortunately, these packages were already installed. In order to access the most recent version of spict that, among others, allows us to plot several scenarios at once, we will use the development branch.


Code
devtools::install_github("DTUAqua/spict/spict", ref = "dev")


Test run spict

Testing SPiCT
Finally, we check that the last version of spict has been correctly installed. We call the data pre-loaded in the package, pol.


Code
library(spict)
data(pol)
inp <- pol$hake
inp$dteuler =1/4
rep1 <- fit.spict(inp)
inp$priors$logbkfrac <- c(log(0.3), 0.1, 1)
rep2 <- fit.spict(inp)
plotspict.compare(list(def = rep1, bkprior = rep2))


Literature related to SPiCT can be found in SPiCT Github under the headline ‘Help files’, including:

section: JABBA: Just Another Bayesian Biomass Assessment
text:
JABBA: Just Another Bayesian Biomass Assessment
JABBA is a surplus production stock assessment model, including projections, retrospective analysis, and hindcasting (forecasting skills).
Further details are presented in the paper of JABBA
Additionally, you can find here a further JABBA development incorporating life history and fisheries’ selectivity into surplus production models:
JABBA-Select
Some examples of JABBA for formal stock assessment in ICCAT are found below:

Mediterranean albacore
South Atlantic albacore
Mediterranean swordfish

Before installing JABBA download and install JAGS. This is very quick.
Next install JABBA from github


Code
devtools::install_github("jabbamodel/JABBA")


Test run JABBA


Code
library(JABBA)
jbinput <- build_jabba(catch=iccat$bet$catch,cpue=iccat$bet$cpue,se=iccat$bet$se,model.type="Schaefer",verbose=F)
bet1 = fit_jabba(jbinput,quickmcmc=FALSE,verbose=FALSE)
p = jbplot_summary(bet1,verbose = F)

title: Installation guide
text:
JARA: Just Another Red-list Assessment
JARA is a Bayesian state-space trend analysis tool. This tool was developed to support decisions regarding the extinction risk of threatened species, incorporating process error and uncertainty.
Please find some literature, including a description of the model, applications, and most recent implementation below:

JARA: Just Another Red-List Assessment
Estimating IUCN Red List population reduction: JARA
Half a century of global decline in oceanic sharks and rays
Coupling state-of-the-art modelling tools for better informed Red List assessments of marine fishes
The conservation status and population decline of the African penguin deconstructed in space and time

However, JARA has also established as a tool to create joint CPUE indices from multiple CPUE or survey indices as well as catch reconstructions with missing year/fleet records. For example, JARA can exactly reproduce the Hierarchical analysis of multiple noisy abundance indices by Conn, 2009 to create a joint index with estimated uncertainty
The General Fisheries Commission of the Mediterranean - recently adopted JARA to track the status of Mediterranean stocks

SoMFi 2025

Similarly, the Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the European Commission has adopted JARA for monitoring trends in stock status against the Common Fisheries Policy

Winker et al. 2022. Suitability study of the Bayesian State-Space model ‘JARA’ for stock status indicator estimation (STECF-Adhoc-22-02)
JRC 2024 Monitoring the Performance of the Common Fisheries Policy (STECF-Adhoc-24-01)
Winker H, Cardinale M, Gerritsen H, Herrera JG, Castellanos P, Farias I, Sampedro P, Moura T, Mosqueira I, Kell L. The ICES MSY approach to reference point estimation is not precautionary. ICES Journal of Marine Science. 2025 Nov;82(11):fsaf204.

Like JABBA, JARA requires JAGS to be installed


Code
devtools::install_github("henning-winker/JARA")


Test run JARA


Code
library(JARA)

data(jaradata)
inp = jrdat$Yellowspot_skate
buildjr <- build_jara(I = inp$I,se=inp$SE,GL=12,silent = T)
fitjr <- fit_jara(buildjr,silent = T)

jrplot_fits(fitjr,silent = T)
jrplot_jointindex(fitjr)




Code
library(JARA)
jrplot_fits(fitjr,silent = T)
jrplot_jointindex(fitjr)

Once we have confirmed that all packages that will be used during the course have been installed and working properly, we could want to review the session information. Thus, we take a look at the version of all installed packages.
If you managed to successfully run the whole script of this guideline, congratulations!. So, you can confirm that your computer is ready to have fun running stock assessments.


Code
sessionInfo()


If you are facing difficulty installing any core package of this guideline ( JABBA and SPiCT), please be aware that most of the issues may be related to installing or updating libraries used by these stock assessment packages. The general recommendation is to check in sessionInfo of this guideline and compare it with the version of those installed in your laptop. So you may update packages accordingly. Additionally, check the Error message provided in the RStudio console to identify what is the issue and act appropriately. Sometimes, deleting the main folder of a given package and installing it from scratch is needed.

title: FLicc
text:
Method overview







Field
Entry




Family / class
Dynamic pool models → equilibrium per-recruit (length-based, single-fleet and multi-gear)


Method name
FLicc (R/FLR/TMB): length-interval catch curves


Short description
Equilibrium length-interval catch curve that explains the length composition of the catch by growth, natural mortality, fishing mortality and gear selectivity, integrated over length bins. LBSPR, LBB and fishblicc are each a configuration of FLicc.


Main outputs
SPR by year with CI, \(F_{SPR}\) reference points, exploitable potential ratio (EPR, the LBB \(B/B_0\)), steepness-corrected \(B/B_{tgt}\), selectivity by gear, length-based indicators (LBIspr, LBImean), yield/SPR contours over selectivity and F.


Typical use case
Length-frequency data by gear and year with life-history information and no reliable index or age data; multi-gear fisheries with asymptotic and dome-shaped selectivity; estimation model in an FLR MSE.



FLicc brings the main lines of length-based per-recruit assessment into one framework, built on FLR and fitted with TMB:







Tool
FLicc configuration




LBSPR
pop_model = "gtg" (ngtg = 13, maxsd = 2, CVL 0.1), obs_model = "mn", Linf, M/k and CVL fixed, by_year = TRUE


LBB
lbb_flicc(): pop_model = "gtg" with ngtg = 1, obs_model = "dm" (fixed precision, ess = 20000), priors on Linf and M/k, by_year = TRUE


fishblicc
pop_model = "gamma", obs_model = "nb", several gears, catch shares in numbers


FLicc default
pop_model = "gtg", obs_model = "dm" with precision estimated (dm_theta = "saturating"), all years jointly with a random walk on F



On this basis FLicc adds what a routine assessment and management procedure needs: several years fitted jointly with shared selectivity, alternative observation models, treatment of the tail of the composition, reference points with steepness, length-based indicators, residual diagnostics, and use as the estimation model of an MSE in FLR.






TipFull documentation



The complete FLicc user guide (H. Winker, FAO-NFI, October 2026) covers the assessment step by step (Part I), the technical options (Part II) and use in MSE (Part III).

title: FLicc
text:
Data requirements







Field
Entry




Minimum data
Length-frequency counts by length bin, year and gear (len, year, data, qname); life history: \(L_\infty\), \(k\), \(M\), \(L_{50}\), length–weight \(a\), \(b\).


Preferred data
Several years per gear with ≥ 50 fish and ≥ 10 bins per gear-year; raw counts or ESS ≥ 500 per gear-year; catch shares by gear (in weight).


Optional auxiliary data
Catch shares by gear; priors on \(L_\infty\) and \(M/k\); external selectivity information; steepness for \(B/B_{tgt}\).


Data quality considerations
Representativeness and sample size per gear-year; consistency of modes and left limbs between years; share of fish at or above \(L_\infty\) (red flag > 1%).




Quick start
# install.packages("TMB", type = "source")
# install.packages(c("FLCore", "ggplotFL"),
#   repos = c("https://flr.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
# remotes::install_github("henning-winker/FLicc")
library(FLicc)

# 1. length data as a long table: len (bin lower bound), year, data (count), qname (gear)
data("alfonsino")
lfd_df <- as.data.frame(lfd_alfonsino)[, c("len", "year", "data", "qname")]

# 2. convert to FLQuants, one per gear
lfd <- FLQuantLen(lfd_long_to_wide(lfd_df), unit = "cm", midL = FALSE)
plot_lfd(lfd)

# 3. life history and stock object
lhpar  <- FLPar(linf = 55.7, k = 0.08, M = 0.162, L50 = 31.1859,
                a = 0.004721956 / 1000, b = 3.146168)
stklen <- stocklen(lfd, lhpar, m_model = "constant")

# 4. fit: one selectivity shape and one catch share (by weight) per gear
fit <- fiticc(lfd, stklen,
              sel_fun = c("dsnormal", "logistic"),
              catch_by_gear = c(0.95, 0.05),
              settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"))

# 5. check and report
flicc_convergence(fit)
plot_len(fit); plot_sel(fit); plot_spr(fit, ci = TRUE)
sprcur_flicc(fit)

Model documentation







Field
Entry




Key parameters
F by year (random walk, sigmaF), selectivity parameters per gear, Dirichlet-multinomial precision; fixed \(L_\infty\), CVL, \(M\), \(k\).


Priors / fixed inputs
Growth (\(L_\infty\), CVL) and M fixed by default; optional priors (linf.sd); sigmaF fixed at 0.3 by default.


Error structure
Observation error: multinomial (mn), Dirichlet-multinomial (dm, default, precision estimated) or negative binomial (nb).

title: FLicc
text:
Assumptions and sensitivities







Field
Entry




Core assumptions
Equilibrium within each year (constant recruitment and mortality), von Bertalanffy growth with variability among growth-type groups, selectivity constant over the years fitted, representative length samples.


Main sensitivities
\(L_\infty\) (the main one), dome-shaped vs logistic selectivity, CVL, tail cut, effective sample size.


Likely violations
Recruitment pulses and cohort signals; changing gear mix or selectivity; non-representative sampling; \(L_\infty\) inconsistent with the data.


Expected bias
The equilibrium model tends to be pessimistic during a rebuild and optimistic while F is increasing; unsupported domes inflate SPR.


Warning signs
Failed convergence checks, narrow or unsupported domes, systematic residuals or failed runs test, retrospective rho beyond ±0.2, gears disagreeing on status.




Checks and red flags

Check
Red flag

1
Sample size by gear-year (plot_lfdn)

3

4

5

Restarts; simplify; tail cut

Recommended defaults







Topic
Recommendation




Observation model
dm with real data


Sample size
dm with dm_theta = "saturating" on raw counts or ESS ≥ 500; with fixed precision or mn, ESS about 150–200 per gear-year


Single year
mn (ESS 150–200 per gear) or dm with dm_theta = "fixed"


Growth
Fix \(L_\infty\) and CVL; \(L_\infty\) is the main sensitivity; default maxsd = 3, ngtg = 13


Selectivity
Logistic unless supported; always run dome_sens_flicc()


Sensitivity runs
fits_summary() for the table; ensemble_flicc() with equal weights


F over time
Random walk, sigmaF fixed (0.3 or the estimate)


Tail
tail_cut at about 0.80–0.85 × \(L_\infty\), as a length


Missing data
Keep zeros, rely on the random walk


Status
SPR at the year’s F; s for \(B/B_{tgt}\) under Beverton–Holt; plot_LBAdvice(flicc2FLStockR(fit))


MSE
Fixed sigmaF, absolute tail cut, se = FALSE; tune with the HCR

Estimation and penalties
SPiCT is not a fully Bayesian model in the same sense as JABBA. Priors or penalties in SPiCT enter the likelihood as additional probability components or constraints. They can stabilize estimation, regularize weakly identified parameters and reflect external information, but the resulting inference is still likelihood-based rather than posterior Bayesian inference.
This distinction should be made clearly in the guide:

in JABBA, priors define probability distributions and inference is based on the posterior;
in SPiCT, prior-like terms are treated as penalties or likelihood components in a maximum-likelihood framework.

In practice, the distinction can become blurred in low-information assessments because both Bayesian priors and frequentist penalties regularize weakly identified models. However, the interpretation of uncertainty differs.

Common prior and penalty options
The specific options depend on SPiCT version and implementation details, but several practical categories are commonly explored within assessments.
Recommended considerations include:

Initial depletion assumptions: assumptions regarding initial biomass relative to carrying capacity (\(B_1/K\)) can strongly influence model trajectories when the catch series does not begin near the start of exploitation. Where early catches are low and the fishery developed gradually, relatively high initial depletion (e.g. \(B_1/K=0.9\)) assumptions may be appropriate. Where substantial exploitation had already occurred before the beginning of the catch series, lower depletion scenarios should also be explored. In SPiCT, \(B_1/K\) can be attempted to be estimated without prior. In some case, a vaguegly informative prior (e.g. \(log.sd=0.5\)) was then added around the initial unconstrained estimate to stabilise the model for future updates.
Production-shape assumptions: flexible production-shape estimation should generally only be explored when the data contain sufficient contrast. Schaefer production functions are often used as reference scenarios because they provide stable and interpretable reference points and considered generally robust for advice. Shape parameters below 1 (i.e. more skewed than a Fox model) were typically not considered in recent benchmark assessments of ICES and GFCM, where a simple Schaefer model is most commonly chosen. Alternative shape assumptions should be compared through production-function plots, diagnostics and sensitivity analyses.
Productivity priors or penalties: intrinsic productivity (\(r\)) is frequently weakly identified, especially when CPUE series are short relative to catch histories. Life-history information can therefore provide useful stabilizing information for defining biologically plausible productivity ranges. Implausibly high productivity estimates should generally be treated cautiously, particularly for long-lived or low-productivity species. All recent benchmark assessments in ICES and GFCM considered informative priors on \(r\).
Process variance assumptions: assumptions regarding process variance can influence biomass flexibility, uncertainty propagation and retrospective behaviour. Very low process variance assumptions may over-constrain biomass trajectories, whereas highly flexible process variance assumptions may allow unrealistic fluctuations. Alternative process-variance assumptions should therefore be explored where diagnostics or retrospective analyses indicate instability.
Observation variance assumptions: CPUE variance assumptions, additional variance estimation and relative weighting among indices can substantially affect model fits and uncertainty estimates. Indices with uncertain standardization or inconsistent temporal coverage may require more conservative observation-error assumptions.
Parameter bounds and constraints: practical estimation bounds are sometimes required to avoid implausible parameter combinations or unstable optimization behaviour, particularly in low-information situations. However, strongly restrictive bounds should be avoided unless supported by biological or fishery knowledge.
Penalty strength and regularization: SPiCT uses a penalized likelihood framework in which penalties may help stabilize estimation and avoid unrealistic parameter combinations. Penalty assumptions should therefore be evaluated carefully to ensure that model behaviour remains driven primarily by the observed data rather than excessive regularization.

These assumptions should generally be treated as sensitivity axes rather than fixed truths. The objective is not to identify a single “best” configuration, but rather to evaluate the robustness, plausibility and consistency of alternative model formulations.

title: Surplus production models
text:
Surplus production models (SPMs) are used where catch histories and one or more relative abundance indices are available but age-structured data are absent, incomplete or not reliable enough for an integrated assessment. They are central to data-limited and data-moderate assessments in many regions, where many stocks with heterogeneous data quality must be assessed.
Good practice for applying SPMs follows Kokkalis et al. (2024); see the model acceptance checklist.
This page sets out the concepts shared by the SPMs in the catalogue (SPiCT, JABBA and BSM/CMSY+): the biomass dynamic logic, the state-space formulation, and the assumptions and caveats common to all of them.

title: Surplus production models
text:
Conceptual model

Biomass dynamic logic
All three approaches considered here belong to the same general family of biomass dynamic models. They represent the stock using an aggregated biomass state and describe changes in biomass as the balance between biological production and removals by fishing.
For the Schaefer form, the deterministic biomass process can be written as:
\[
B_{t+1} = B_t + r B_t \left(1 - \frac{B_t}{K}\right) - C_t,
\]
where \(B_t\) is biomass in year \(t\), \(r\) is the intrinsic rate of population increase, \(K\) is carrying capacity, and \(C_t\) is catch or removals.
The abundance index is typically linked to biomass through a catchability parameter:
\[
I_t = q B_t \exp(\eta_t),
\]
where \(I_t\) is the observed CPUE or survey index, \(q\) is catchability, and \(\eta_t\) is observation error.
Under the Schaefer production model, the common MSY reference points are:
\[
B_{MSY} = \frac{K}{2}, \quad F_{MSY} = \frac{r}{2}, \quad MSY = \frac{rK}{4}.
\]
Alternative production functions, such as Fox or Pella-Tomlinson forms, change the shape of the production curve and therefore the position of \(B_{MSY}\) relative to \(K\).


Production function as the central interpretive figure
For reporting, the production-function plot should be treated as a central cross-model figure. It links the estimated biomass trajectory to the implied surplus production curve and MSY reference points. It is particularly useful because it helps assess whether the data provide sufficient contrast to estimate productivity and depletion.
For SPiCT, the production-function plot is more central than a Kobe plot. SPiCT produces likelihood-based estimates and uncertainty intervals, not posterior probabilities. Kobe-style summaries may be useful descriptively, but they should not be framed as posterior Kobe probabilities.
For JABBA, the Kobe plot has a stronger probabilistic interpretation because stock status probabilities are derived from the joint posterior distribution of biomass and fishing-mortality or harvest-rate states.

title: Surplus production models
text:
State-space surplus production models

Why state-space models?
A key advance in modern SPMs is the separation of the true but unobserved stock trajectory from noisy observations. In a state-space model, biomass is a latent state, while CPUE or survey indices are observations of that latent state.
The process model describes how biomass changes through time:
\[
B_{t+1} = f(B_t, C_t, \theta) \exp(\varepsilon_t),
\]
where \(f(\cdot)\) is the deterministic biomass update function and \(\varepsilon_t\) is process error.
The observation model describes how indices relate to biomass:
\[
I_t = q B_t \exp(\eta_t),
\]
where \(\eta_t\) is observation error.
Process error may reflect recruitment variability, environmental variability, natural-mortality variation, growth variation, changes in availability, and structural mismatch between the simple biomass model and the true age-, size- or spatially structured population. Observation error reflects sampling error, CPUE standardization uncertainty, reporting error, and unmodelled variation in catchability.


Process error: practical interpretation
Process error should be explained pragmatically rather than treated as a technical debate about the exact placement of the error term. The most important messages are:

process error allows the biomass trajectory to deviate from the deterministic production curve;
this is realistic because real stocks do not follow smooth deterministic trajectories;
estimating process and observation error simultaneously is difficult in low-information assessments;
process-error assumptions can strongly influence stock trajectories, uncertainty and forecasts;
estimated process error should be biologically plausible and should be evaluated through diagnostics and sensitivity analyses.

Process error should not be interpreted simply as “noise”. In an SPM it absorbs both natural population variability and structural limitations of the model. This is important because SPMs do not explicitly represent age structure, size structure, spatial dynamics, recruitment pulses, changing selectivity or changes in catchability.


Plausible magnitude of process error
The likely magnitude of process error depends on life history, recruitment variability, exploitation level and the degree to which the biomass model approximates the true stock dynamics.
Short-lived species and small pelagics are expected to show larger process variation than long-lived demersal or deep-water species. Process variation may also increase under heavy fishing because age truncation makes biomass more sensitive to recruitment variability.
This concept should be used qualitatively to motivate sensitivity analyses. For example:

small pelagics may justify higher process-error assumptions;
long-lived coastal or demersal species may justify lower process-error assumptions;
strongly depleted stocks may require wider process-error sensitivity ranges;
short CPUE series may not contain enough information to estimate process and observation error reliably.

title: Surplus production models
section: Assumptions and caveats common to surplus production models
text:
Assumptions and caveats common to surplus production models
SPiCT and JABBA differ in estimation philosophy and time structure, but they share most of the core assumptions and limitations of surplus production models. These assumptions should therefore be evaluated carefully when interpreting stock status, reference points and management advice.

Aggregated biomass representation: surplus production models summarize the stock as a single biomass state and do not explicitly model age structure, length structure, sex structure or spatial structure. This parsimony can be advantageous in data-limited situations, but may also obscure important biological processes and population dynamics.
Selectivity and catchability assumptions: surplus production models generally assume that abundance indices remain proportional to exploitable biomass through time. This assumption may be violated by changing fleet behaviour, technological creep, spatial targeting, hyperstability, hyperdepletion, changing selectivity, changes in species composition or expansion and contraction of fishing grounds. In many practical applications, these issues may influence model behaviour more strongly than the choice between SPiCT and JABBA.
Lag effects and delayed population responses: surplus production models do not explicitly represent lagged relationships between recruitment, spawning biomass and exploitable biomass. For medium- and long-lived species, strong recruitment events or recruitment failures may only influence exploitable biomass several years later. Within surplus production models, these effects are typically absorbed into process variability or may appear as model misspecification.
Stationary productivity assumptions: surplus production models generally assume that the underlying production relationship remains stationary through time. This assumption may be violated under climate-driven productivity shifts, ecosystem changes, regime shifts or persistent changes in recruitment dynamics.
Data contrast requirements: reliable estimation of productivity and depletion requires sufficient contrast in catch and abundance-index data. Long catch histories combined with short CPUE series may still provide useful information, but can also allow multiple plausible depletion trajectories. Short, flat or contradictory CPUE series are particularly challenging and may reduce parameter identifiability and prediction skill.

These assumptions should not necessarily be interpreted as reasons to reject surplus production models. Rather, they define the conditions under which results should be interpreted cautiously and evaluated through diagnostics, hindcast validation and sensitivity analyses. ### Data contrast
SPMs require contrast in catch and abundance data to estimate productivity and depletion. Long catch series with short CPUE series can be informative, but may also allow multiple plausible depletion histories. Short, flat or contradictory CPUE series are particularly challenging.

title: Sensitivity analysis
text:
Sensitivity analysis should be treated as a required component of the assessment process rather than a small number of optional exploratory runs. The objective is to evaluate whether key assessment conclusions remain robust under plausible alternative assumptions.
Typical sensitivity analyses include:

Initial depletion: alternative assumptions for \(B_1/K\) or \(\psi\), particularly when the catch series does not begin near the start of exploitation.
Productivity: alternative priors or penalties on \(r\), especially for long-lived or low-productivity species.
Process error: alternative assumptions regarding process variance to evaluate whether model results depend strongly on stochastic biomass flexibility.
Observation error: alternative CPUE variance assumptions, including input CVs, estimated additional variance, or index-specific weighting.
CPUE/index selection: alternative index combinations where indices conflict or differ substantially in standardization quality.
Catch history: alternative catch reconstructions or historical-removal scenarios where catches are uncertain or incompletely reconstructed.
Production-shape assumption: alternative Schaefer, Fox or Pella-Tomlinson production functions where biologically plausible, while retaining the Schaefer formulation as a transparent reference scenario.

Sensitivity analyses should not be interpreted as attempts to identify a single “best” model, but rather as a structured evaluation of the robustness, plausibility and management consistency of alternative assessment assumptions.

title: Diagnostics and model validation
text:
Why diagnostics matter
Modern SPM workflows should not stop at a base-case fit. A model can fit the observed CPUE but still provide poor advice if the fit is achieved through overfitting, implausible process error, unsuitable priors, or unrecognized data conflicts.
The diagnostic framework should evaluate four broad properties:

Convergence: did the optimizer or MCMC estimation behave adequately?
Fit to data: are residuals acceptable and broadly random?
Model consistency: are estimates stable under retrospective peels?
Prediction skill: can the model predict withheld observations?
Plausibility: does the model predict a realistic biological state that is consistent with the exploitation history?

Modern diagnostics should therefore not focus solely on goodness-of-fit. Contemporary assessment frameworks increasingly evaluate models according to multiple complementary dimensions.
A useful conceptual framework is shown below.








Figure 1





Residual diagnostics
Residual diagnostics evaluate whether the fitted model systematically over- or under-predicts observations.
For CPUE or survey indices, the guide should include:

residual plots by index;
joint residual plots across indices;
RMSE summaries;
runs tests for non-random residual sequences;
outlier checks;
comparison of residual patterns across model scenarios.

A good fit to residuals is necessary but not sufficient. Residuals can improve when extra parameters are added, even if prediction skill deteriorates.
Retrospective analysis
Retrospective analysis evaluates the stability of model-derived quantities as recent years of data are sequentially removed. It is useful for identifying systematic changes in estimates of stock status or fishing mortality when new data are added.
However, retrospective analysis uses latent model quantities such as biomass or fishing mortality. These quantities are not observed directly. Therefore, retrospective stability alone is not validation.
In the guide, retrospective analysis should be interpreted as a model-consistency diagnostic, not as the final model-acceptance test.
Hindcast cross-validation
Hindcast cross-validation evaluates prediction skill by withholding observations from the terminal period, fitting the model to the truncated dataset, and comparing model predictions to the withheld observations.
This is critical because it evaluates the model against observations that were not used for fitting.
The basic workflow is:

remove the most recent observation from one or more CPUE/index series;
refit the model;
predict the withheld observation;
compare predicted and observed values;
repeat for multiple peels and prediction horizons;
summarize prediction residuals and prediction skill.

This can be applied to CPUE, survey indices and, where relevant, empirical composition summaries such as mean length or mean age.
MASE metric: mean absolute scaled error
A practical prediction-skill metric is the mean absolute scaled error (MASE). It compares the model prediction error to a naïve baseline forecast, typically the previous observation.
Interpretation:

\(MASE < 1\): the model predicts better than the naïve baseline;
\(MASE = 1\): the model predicts about as well as the naïve baseline;
\(MASE > 1\): the model predicts worse than the naïve baseline;
\(MASE = 0.5\): the model is approximately twice as accurate as the naïve baseline.

This makes MASE useful because it is interpretable and can be compared across indices with different scales.

title: Data preparation workflow
text:
Draft
Fishery data are often used at face value as inputs to data-limited assessments or indicator-based frameworks, without first being explored and critically reviewed. Biased inputs lead to biased status and misdirected management. This workflow is the step that comes before the decision framework and any method. It follows FAO Fisheries and Aquaculture Technical Paper 706 (Amoroso et al., 2024), with its Excel templates and the FishualizeR app as tools.

title: Data preparation workflow
section: Checks that most often change the assessment
text:
Checks that most often change the assessment

Coverage: gaps in years, areas or gears. A length composition from one port or one gear is not the catch composition of the stock.
Changes on the timeline: a new gear, regulation or reporting system can create a step in CPUE or length data that is not a change in abundance.
Length compositions: at least about 50 fish and 10 length bins per gear and year; consistent units; no fish far beyond \(L_\infty\).
Catch: under-reporting, missing fleets (small-scale, recreational, IUU) and species aggregated as “nei”.
CPUE: changes in targeting, fleet composition or technology. Nominal CPUE should not go into an assessment without standardisation.
Short index, long exploitation history: complement with local knowledge and alternative sources (export records, vessel registries). Expert knowledge can reveal early depletion that official series miss.

text:
Method overview



Field
Entry




Family / class

Method name
cpueTargeting (R): Henning-Winker/cpueTargeting · project page


Short description
Toolbox for standardising real multispecies catch and effort data where targeting changes over time, plus operating models that test how well standardisation copes with targeting.


Main outputs
Standardised CPUE index with log SE and CV for the assessment (export_index()), model comparison, influence and step plots, residual and predictive checks, processing log.


Typical use case
Commercial logbook or observer CPUE from multispecies or multi-tactic fisheries, before it is used as an index in SPiCT, JABBA, BSM or an empirical rule.



Author: Henning Winker (FAO NFIFM). The package has two parts: operating models that simulate fisheries with changing targeting, so that standardisation methods can be tested against a known truth, and a step-by-step toolbox for real data.







Step
Functions




1. Format: one row per operation, synonyms, processing log
cpue_data(), subset(), cpue_matrix()


2. Fleet: operations by year and vessel, indicator vessels, vessel profiles
plot_fleet(), vessel_summary(), select_vessels(), plot_vessel_profile()


3. Species: cumulative species curves and the species set
species_curve(), plot_species_curve(), select_species()


4. Nominal CPUE and catch composition
nominal_cpue(), plot_nominal(), plot_composition(), plot_cpue_map()


5. Subsetting: habitat-based (Stephens and MacCall), removing irrelevant tactics
stephens_maccall(), plot_stephens_maccall(), select_tactics()


6. Targeting covariates: composition PCA, Optimal Coordinates test, clustering
add_targeting(), composition_pca(), compute_oc(), cluster_tactics(), tactic_table()


7. Models (mgcv): Base, Covariates, DPC, Cluster, spatial, random vessel effects
fit_cpue()


8. Diagnostics: model table, influence, step plot, residuals, predictive check
cpue_diagnostics(), plot_step(), plot_influence(), plot_residuals(), ppc_cpue()


9. Index for the assessment, with log SE and CV
cpue_index(), export_index()

Positions, month, gear or hook configuration; several years of indicator vessels; full species composition of each operation.

Field

cpue_data() to one row per operation with synonyms resolved; select_vessels(), select_species(); every selection is recorded in x$log.


Standardization needs
This is the standardisation step: Base, Covariates, Cluster and DPC (direct principal components) GAMs, optional spatial terms and random vessel effects; Tweedie or delta families.


Aggregation / binning choices
To be completed Documents how catches, ages or lengths should be grouped.

Indicator fleets by activity and target-species rules; fishing tactics from clustering the catch composition; habitat-based subsetting (Stephens and MacCall 2004).

library(cpueTargeting)
x <- cpue_data(logbook, year = "year", species = "species", catch = "kg",
               effort = "hours", id = "trip", vessel = "vessel", covariates = "month")
x <- select_species(x, threshold = 0.95, keep = "Pagellus bogaraveo")
x <- add_targeting(x)          # PCs (Optimal Coordinates test) and clusters
fit <- fit_cpue(x, species = "Pagellus bogaraveo",
                models = c("Base", "Covariates", "Cluster", "DPC"), vessel = TRUE)
cpue_diagnostics(fit)
export_index(fit, "cpue_index.csv", model = "DPC")   # index with log SE for SPiCT/JABBA

title: cpueTargeting
text:
Assumptions and sensitivities







Field
Entry




Core assumptions
Targeting is captured by the catch composition (PCs or clusters); the reference set of covariates is constant over time; the indicator fleet samples the stock consistently.


Main sensitivities
Species set, number of PCs and clusters, error family, habitat subsetting.


Likely violations
Persistent changes in relative abundance of the species in the composition; shifts in fishing grounds outside the data; technology creep.


Expected bias
When relative abundances change persistently, PCs can absorb part of the real trend of the species whose abundance changes most (more PCs absorb more); coarser clusters are less affected.


Warning signs
Large influence of targeting terms in years where the trend changes; poor predictive check of zeros or tails by year; index follows nominal CPUE of a single tactic.

Method name
FishualizeR: R Shiny app accompanying FAO Fisheries and Aquaculture Technical Paper 706 (code: DanOvando/fishualizeR; app: apps.upwellsolutionsllc.com/app/FishualizeR)


Short description
Interactive app that walks users through common visualisation and quality control of fisheries length data, and aggregates it into length compositions.


Main outputs
Plots of raw data (with colour and faceting options), data-coverage metrics over time or location, and length compositions in user-defined bins, all downloadable.


Typical use case
First look at length samples before a length-based assessment (FLicc, LBSPR, LBB): check units, gaps and coverage, then bin by year, area or gear.



FishualizeR was developed (led by Brian Snouffer, Upwell Solutions) to support FAO Technical Paper 706, which sets out the data-preparation workflow: data inventory, timeline of influential events, life-history parameter inventory, cleaning and outlier handling, and exploratory data analysis. The app supports four steps: (1) upload length data and fix unit inconsistencies such as cm and mm; (2) plot and examine the raw data; (3) assess coverage over time or location and download coverage metrics; (4) aggregate into length bins at chosen levels and download the result.

title: Principles
text: The toolbox is built on a hierarchical assessment framework (Kell et al., 2025). Stocks are assessed with whatever data exist, but the assessment logic, the biology and the definition of reference points stay the same as data are added. Advice is then risk-equivalent: the probability of breaching a limit is the same whichever tier a stock is assessed at, with larger precautionary buffers where information is poorer. This puts data-poor and data-moderate stocks on a common footing instead of treating them as separate, incomparable worlds.

title: Principles
text:
One logic across tiers

Shared biology. Growth, natural mortality, maturity, selectivity and steepness are defined once and used by every tier, so moving up a tier changes the information, not the assumptions.
Unifying model families. On the length side, FLicc reproduces LBSPR, LBB and fishblicc as configurations of one model. FLicc-SPM extends the same model with surplus production dynamics, so that length data, catches and indices enter one likelihood. Unlike a fully structured model it does not fit the catch exactly, and it keeps uncertainty in all fits.
Consistent reference points. FSPR and SPR-based rules at tier 1, and FMSY and BMSY at tiers 2–4, come from the same per-recruit model.

title: Principles
text:
Value of information
Because the tiers share one model and one set of assumptions, the contribution of each data source can be measured directly: run the same stock at each tier and compare how well status and advice recover the truth.

Simulated twins: operating models with known truth (for example the FLicc simulator, the cpueTargeting and mmsyFM operating models) generate catches, indices and length compositions for the same stock.
Metrics by tier: bias and precision of B/BMSY and F/FMSY, probability of misclassifying status, and the buffer needed for risk-equivalent advice, by exploitation phase (fishing down, rebuilding).
Real data: the same comparisons on well-studied stocks (for example ICES case studies) where a data-rich assessment serves as a benchmark.

The answer guides two decisions: which method a stock’s data support now, and which data collection would improve advice most.

title: Principles
text:
One standard of good practice
Risk equivalence only holds if every assessment that informs advice, at every tier, has passed the same standard of scrutiny. The toolbox adopts the four objective properties of a plausible model (Carvalho et al., 2021): convergence, fit to the data, model consistency and prediction skill, with plausibility (consistency with the biology and the exploitation history) as the overarching check. No single diagnostic is used in isolation to accept or reject a model. For surplus production models these are made operational in the good practice guidelines of Kokkalis et al. (2024); the model acceptance checklist applies them across the toolbox.

title: Misuse prevention
text:
Pre-run checks
Each catalogue entry now lists pre-run checks: concrete questions an analyst, or an app such as the Stock Monitoring Tool, should answer before a method is run, and what to do if a check fails. The idea goes back to the guidance for uses and misuses of data-limited methods developed by N. Gutierrez and K. Kleisner (2018) for the FAO online modules: for example, at least 20 years of catch with a peak away from the ends of the series before a catch-only method is run, or a representative length sample across habitats and gears before ELEFAN. The CMSY+ page includes an interactive catch-series check that applies these rules.

title: Misuse prevention
text:
General red flags

Status depends mostly on priors or fixed inputs rather than data (prior and posterior nearly identical).
Good fit to data but poor prediction skill (hindcast MASE > 1).
Strong retrospective patterns (Mohn’s rho beyond about ±0.2).
Results inconsistent with the exploitation history or the biology of the stock.
A single “best” run reported without sensitivity analysis.

title: NFIFM Toolbox
text:
Development version. NFIFM Toolbox is a working title for the shared method library of the FAO Global Stock Assessment Capacity Programme. Content is draft and not an official FAO product.
The toolbox is the shared method library and code of the programme’s cross-regional learning hub. It helps national and regional analysts pick an assessment method that fits their data, prepare the data properly, run and diagnose the assessment, and turn results into management advice. It is used across the regional implementation platforms and reports into SOFIA, FIRMS and SDG 14.4.1.
Every method is documented the same way. Each page covers data requirements, assumptions, diagnostics, worked examples and code, and has an explicit misuse prevention section: when not to use the method, common misuses, and checks to pass before results are used for advice.

title: NFIFM Toolbox
text:
Philosophy
The toolbox follows a hierarchical assessment framework: one assessment logic and one set of biological assumptions across the data ladder, from length data only to catch, length and abundance indices; risk-equivalent advice whichever tier a stock is assessed at; and the value of information of each data source measured in simulated and real case studies.

title: CMSY+
text:
Assumptions and sensitivities







Field
Entry




Core assumptions
Schaefer production; stationary productivity (constant parameters); complete catch series; depletion priors reflect the true start and end state.


Main sensitivities
Lower bound of the r prior; start and final depletion priors; upper bound on k in developing fisheries.


Likely violations
Incomplete or under-reported catches; catches driven by markets or regulation rather than abundance; developing fisheries without a peak; lightly exploited stocks.


Expected bias
Evaluations found k overestimated by about 10% and r (and FMSY) underestimated, closer to F0.1 (after Gutierrez and Kleisner, 2018); with short or incomplete catch series, status can be biased in either direction.


Warning signs
Posterior close to the depletion prior; r estimate at the lower prior bound; very wide range of viable r–k pairs.

title: CMSY+
text:
Misuse prevention






WarningMisuse warnings shown by the method selector




Do not use: when catch = incomplete: Catch-only methods assume the catch series is complete. Under-reported or missing catches bias productivity and depletion directly.
Caution: when goal = catch advice: Catch-only status is driven largely by priors on depletion and resilience. It should not be the sole basis for catch advice.
Caution: when lifehistory = short-lived: Short-lived, recruitment-driven stocks fluctuate strongly; catch-only depletion priors are rarely informative for them.
Caution: when goal = HCR testing: An assessment fit alone does not test a harvest control rule. Use the assessment as the estimation model in an MSE (see FLR mse).
Do not use: when catch_pattern = short: Catch-only methods need at least about 20 years of catch covering development, peak and decline; shorter or flat series contain too little information on productivity (Gutierrez and Kleisner, 2018).
Do not use: when catch_pattern = increasing: In a developing fishery with still-increasing catches the peak has not been reached, so carrying capacity cannot be bounded from the catch.
Do not use: when catch_pattern = light: Lightly exploited stocks: the catch series carries almost no information on productivity.
Caution: when catch = reliable: Depletion priors derived only from the ratio of recent to maximum catch are assumptions, not data; set them with expert input or length and CPUE evidence where possible.

Rules are maintained in data/misuse_rules.csv.

Caution: when index_type = commercial: Commercial CPUE may be hyperstable or affected by changing targeting. Standardise it (see cpueTargeting) before use.
Caution: when species = mixed: Single-species production models ignore technical interactions; reference points may not be jointly achievable in mixed fisheries.
Caution: when goal = HCR testing: An assessment fit alone does not test a harvest control rule. Use the assessment as the estimation model in an MSE (see FLR mse).

Method name

Short description
Bayesian state-space surplus production model fitted by MCMC, estimating biomass dynamics, process and observation error, reference points and stock status.


Main outputs
Posterior biomass, depletion and harvest-rate trajectories; MSY reference points; Kobe probabilities; projections and risk tables.


Typical use case

JABBA, Just Another Bayesian Biomass Assessment, is a Bayesian state-space surplus production model implemented in R/JAGS. It estimates biomass dynamics, process error, observation error, reference points and stock status using MCMC. JABBA has been widely used in tuna, billfish, shark and coastal fish assessments, often in contexts with long catch histories and shorter CPUE series.
JABBA is particularly useful where:

prior information is important;
uncertainty needs to be expressed probabilistically;
posterior stock-status probabilities are required;
multiple CPUE series need to be fitted;
scenario testing and ensemble-style assessment are central;
Kobe plots and risk tables are required for management interpretation.

Posterior interpretation
JABBA outputs should be interpreted as posterior distributions. This allows direct calculation of probabilities such as:

probability that \(B/B_{MSY} < 1\);
probability that \(F/F_{MSY} > 1\);
probability of being in each Kobe quadrant;
probability that catch advice achieves a specified risk threshold.

This is a major distinction from SPiCT. JABBA’s Kobe plot is a posterior probability summary, while SPiCT’s status plot is likelihood-based and should be presented accordingly.

Common prior options
JABBA provides substantial flexibility for incorporating prior information within a Bayesian state-space framework. Prior assumptions can strongly influence model behaviour in low-information situations and should therefore be documented transparently and explored through sensitivity analyses.
Recommended considerations include:

Initial depletion priors: assumptions regarding initial biomass relative to carrying capacity (\(\psi = B_1/K\)) can strongly influence estimated biomass trajectories, particularly when catch histories begin after substantial exploitation has already occurred. Where historical catches begin close to the onset of exploitation and early catches are low, relatively high initial depletion assumptions may be appropriate. Where fisheries were already substantially developed at the start of the catch series, lower initial depletion scenarios should also be explored.
Productivity priors: intrinsic productivity (\(r\)) is commonly informed using life-history characteristics, resilience classifications or previous assessments. Long-lived, slow-growing species generally require lower productivity assumptions than short-lived or highly productive species. Alternative productivity priors should usually be evaluated through sensitivity analyses, particularly where abundance indices are short relative to catch histories.
Carrying capacity priors: assumptions regarding carrying capacity (\(K\)) can influence depletion estimates and biomass scaling, especially where abundance indices contain limited contrast. Very broad priors may lead to unstable or weakly identified biomass trajectories, whereas overly restrictive priors may constrain the model unrealistically. Priors should therefore remain biologically plausible while allowing reasonable flexibility.
Production-shape assumptions: Schaefer, Fox or Pella-Tomlinson production functions may imply substantially different production dynamics and reference points. Schaefer-type production functions are often useful as transparent reference scenarios, while more flexible shape assumptions should generally only be interpreted cautiously unless the data provide sufficient contrast.
Process variance priors: assumptions regarding stochastic biomass variability influence uncertainty propagation, retrospective behaviour and stock-status trajectories. Very low process variance assumptions may over-constrain biomass dynamics, whereas very high process variance may allow unrealistic biomass flexibility. Alternative process-variance assumptions should therefore be explored where diagnostics or retrospective patterns suggest instability.
Observation variance priors: assumptions regarding observation error can substantially influence relative weighting among CPUE or survey indices, particularly when multiple indices differ in quality or standardization approach. Indices with uncertain standardization or limited spatial coverage may require more conservative observation-error assumptions.
Catchability assumptions: priors or constraints on catchability coefficients may sometimes be useful where abundance indices are poorly scaled or where strong prior knowledge regarding relative index behaviour exists. Abrupt or implausible catchability estimates may indicate problems with index standardization or insufficient contrast in the data.
Priors for poorly identified parameters: informative priors may help stabilize estimation where catches and abundance indices alone provide insufficient contrast to estimate parameters robustly. However, strongly informative priors should be interpreted cautiously and evaluated through posterior diagnostics and sensitivity analyses to ensure that assessment conclusions are not driven primarily by prior assumptions.

Because JABBA estimates full posterior distributions, prior assumptions should always be evaluated carefully through posterior diagnostics and sensitivity analyses. Particular attention should be given to situations where posterior estimates remain strongly influenced by prior assumptions rather than the observed data.

title: Length-based and per-recruit methods
text:
Equilibrium per-recruit methods evaluate the expected contribution of an average recruit under assumed constant conditions. Length-based variants infer fishing mortality relative to natural mortality from the length composition of the catch, together with growth and maturity. They are the main option where only length data and life-history information are available, which is common in small-scale fisheries (workstream 2).
FLicc brings LBSPR, LBB and fishblicc into one framework: each is a configuration of FLicc, reproduced on its own example data in the FLicc user guide.






WarningShared caveats




Equilibrium: status lags behind changes in F or recruitment.
Selectivity: pooling gears with different selectivity biases SPR; dome-shaped selectivity must be supported by data.
Life history: results are most sensitive to \(L_\infty\) and \(M/k\); proxies need sensitivity runs.
Sampling: length samples must represent the catch of each gear.

text:
Assumptions and sensitivities







Field
Entry




Core assumptions
Length frequencies represent the population (all ages, areas and habitats sampled); growth follows a (seasonal) von Bertalanffy curve; mortality and recruitment are constant (equilibrium).


Main sensitivities
Moving-average span and bin width; search ranges for \(L_\infty\) and \(K\); \(M\) estimator; seasonal growth on or off.


Likely violations
Emigration from the fishing grounds (overestimates Z); strong sexual dimorphism in size (biases growth); juveniles and adults in different habitats with sampling in only one of them.


Expected bias
Wrong growth parameters propagate into \(Z\), \(M\) and status; under emigration \(Z\) is overestimated.


Warning signs
ELEFAN score surface flat or with several peaks; \(L_\infty\) at a search bound; growth curves not following visible modes.

WarningMisuse warnings shown by the method selector

Caution: when gears = multiple: ELEFAN and the catch curve assume one selectivity; pooled gears blur the growth modes and the catch curve. Analyse a single gear.
Caution: when lifehistory = long-lived: ELEFAN needs clear modal progression; for slow-growing, long-lived species the length modes overlap and growth estimates are unreliable. Prefer independent growth estimates.

Length samples come from one habitat or gear that misses part of the population; modes are not visible (slow growth, long-lived species); several gears with different selectivity are pooled.

Accepting the first ELEFAN solution without checking the score surface; using one empirical \(M\); reading \(F_{current} > F_{0.1}\) as precise status.

To be completed Minimum checks to pass before results are used for advice.


Pre-run checks
Is the length-frequency sample representative of the whole population? Are all age groups sampled? Were samples taken across the areas where different life stages live (e.g. juveniles nearshore, adults offshore)? Were gears with different selectivity used, so that several age groups appear? If not, F estimates will be biased (after Gutierrez and Kleisner, 2018).

Not every stock can be assessed with a model, and models are not the only evidence. Fishery indicators summarise what the data and the fishery’s history say directly: how the catch developed, where catch rates and effort are heading, what the size structure shows, and what fishers observe. Indicators show direction and pattern, rarely a sustainable catch level; catch advice needs an empirical rule tuned by simulation or an assessment.

text:
Assumptions and sensitivities







Field
Entry




Core assumptions
Schaefer production for each stock; catchability by métier constant over time; effort allocated by expected profit; stock parameters (\(r\), \(K\), depletion) taken from assessments.


Main sensitivities
Catchability matrix, profit preference \(\gamma\), prices and costs, stock productivity and depletion used for conditioning.


Likely violations
Catchability changing with technology or targeting; stocks whose dynamics are poorly described by Schaefer production; prices and costs that shift effort in ways not modelled.


Expected bias
If \(r\) and \(K\) are taken from weak assessments, the MMSY and the risk of breaching Bpa inherit their bias; a shared-q simplification forces all rules along one line (\(F_i/F_j = q_i/q_j\)).


Warning signs
Status quo that cannot be tuned to observed effort and depletions; MMSY that requires effort far outside historical levels; decision tables dominated by one stock at its safeguard.

Methodological literature
text: SPiCT and JABBA are widely documented state-space surplus production model frameworks in fisheries assessment. SPiCT is based on a continuous-time stochastic production model formulation. JABBA is a Bayesian state-space biomass-dynamics framework implemented in JAGS. The peer-reviewed literature includes core model descriptions, practical guidance, time-varying productivity developments, selectivity extensions and risk-equivalence frameworks.

title: Methodological literature
text:
Core references
Pedersen, M.W. and Berg, C.W. 2017. A stochastic surplus production model in continuous time. Fish and Fisheries, 18(2): 226–243. https://doi.org/10.1111/faf.12174

Core SPiCT reference paper.
Introduces the continuous-time stochastic surplus production model.
Separates process variation in stock dynamics from observation error in biomass indices.
Includes fisheries dynamics so that uncertainty in catches can be propagated into estimated parameters and management quantities.

Winker, H., Carvalho, F. and Kapur, M. 2018. JABBA: Just Another Bayesian Biomass Assessment. Fisheries Research, 204: 275–288. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fishres.2018.03.010

Core JABBA reference paper.
Presents an open-source Bayesian state-space biomass-dynamics assessment framework.
Includes alternative production functions, multiple CPUE series, additional observation variance, retrospective diagnostics and projections.
Case study: South Atlantic swordfish.


JABBA-Select extension
Winker, H., Carvalho, F., Thorson, J.T., Kell, L.T., Parker, D., Kapur, M., Sharma, R., Booth, A.J. and Kerwath, S.E. 2020. JABBA-Select: Incorporating life history and fisheries’ selectivity into surplus production models. Fisheries Research, 222: 105355. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fishres.2019.105355

Extends JABBA to account for fisheries selectivity and life-history information.
Distinguishes exploitable biomass from spawning biomass.
Provides a bridge between conventional surplus production models and age-structured production models.
Case study: South African silver kob.



Hierarchical assessment frameworks and risk equivalence
Kell, L.T., Cardinale, M., Mosqueira, I., Winker, H. and Sharma, R. 2025. Transforming Data and Capacity-Limited Stock Assessment: Achieving Risk Equivalence with Hierarchical Assessment Frameworks and Auxiliary Data. Sustainability, 17(21): 9383. https://doi.org/10.3390/su17219383

Methodological synthesis and extension.
Proposes a hierarchical assessment framework (HAF) built around Bayesian state-space biomass dynamic models.
Uses JABBA with auxiliary data to demonstrate the framework.
Evaluates risk equivalence across data-rich and data-limited assessment tiers.
Integrates auxiliary information including fishing mortality indicators, depletion information and length-based metrics into JABBA-type biomass dynamic assessments.
Uses simulation testing conditioned on 82 assessed Northeast Atlantic stocks.



Comparative evaluation and uncertainty literature
Kell, L.T., Sharma, R. and Winker, H. Artefact and Artifice: evaluation of the skill of catch-only methods for classifying stock status.

Comparative paper on assessment skill and classification performance.
Explores JABBA in a catch-only configuration alongside other catch-only assessment methods.
Relevant to model plausibility, structural uncertainty, stock-status misclassification risk and comparative assessment frameworks.



Good-practice reference for SPiCT and JABBA
Kokkalis, A., Berg, C.W., Kapur, M.S., Winker, H., Jacobsen, N.S., Taylor, M.H., Ichinokawa, M., Miyagawa, M., Medeiros-Leal, W., Nielsen, J.R. and Mildenberger, T.K. 2024. Good practices for surplus production models. Fisheries Research, 275: 107010. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fishres.2024.107010

Provides good-practice recommendations for applying surplus production models.
Discusses SPiCT and JABBA.
Covers input data, priors, diagnostics, simulation testing and use of SPMs for advice.



Management strategy evaluation and SPiCT performance testing
Mildenberger, T.K., Berg, C.W., Kokkalis, A., Nielsen, J.R., Punt, A.E. and co-authors. Full citation to be completed once bibliographic details are verified.

Evaluates SPiCT within a management strategy evaluation framework.
Tests harvest control rules and robustness of SPiCT-based management advice.
Links SPiCT to operational management procedures and risk-performance evaluation.



Time-varying productivity extensions
Chang, Y.-J., Winker, H., Sculley, M. and Hsu, J. 2020. Evaluation of the status and risk of overexploitation of the Pacific billfish stocks considering non-stationary population processes. Deep Sea Research Part II: Topical Studies in Oceanography, 175: 104707. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dsr2.2019.104707

Uses the JABBA framework with non-stationary population processes.
Explores implications for biomass trajectories and management reference points.
Illustrates extension of Bayesian surplus production models beyond stationary production assumptions.

Mildenberger, T.K. et al. 2025. Estimating time-varying productivity and reference points: A case of North Sea demersal fish stocks. Fish and Fisheries. https://doi.org/10.1111/faf.12910

Applies a modified SPiCT-type framework with time-varying productivity.
Relevant for cases where productivity and reference points are not stationary.

title: Training and apps
text: The toolbox is closely tied to the programme’s capacity-building work. The Stock Monitoring Tool on the iMarine gateway is the main training environment: trainees run methods there without programming, and use the toolbox pages for the method’s data needs, assumptions, diagnostics and misuse risks. The apps lower the entry barrier; the catalogue pages are what keep their results interpretable.
